clinicalPearls: Trichuriasis is caused by the whipworm Trichuris trichiura, a soil-transmitted nematode acquired by ingesting embryonated eggs from faecally contaminated soil, food or water
The adult worm has a slender whip-like anterior threaded into the colonic mucosa and a thicker posterior end, and lives predominantly in the caecum and ascending colon
Light infections are usually asymptomatic, whereas heavy burdens cause chronic colitis with abdominal pain, tenesmus and mucoid, sometimes bloody, diarrhoea
Massive infection in children can produce the Trichuris dysentery syndrome with rectal prolapse, anaemia and growth and cognitive impairment
Diagnosis is by identifying the characteristic barrel-shaped eggs with bipolar mucous plugs on stool microscopy
Adult worms may be seen on colonoscopy attached to an inflamed mucosa
Albendazole or mebendazole is used, though whipworm responds less reliably to single-dose therapy than other soil-transmitted helminths and may need repeated or combination courses
reference.pathophysiology: Trichuris trichiura eggs passed in faeces embryonate in warm, moist soil and become infective over several weeks; once ingested they hatch in the small intestine and the larvae mature as they move to the large bowel. The adult worm embeds its narrow anterior portion within a syncytial tunnel in the colonic epithelium while its posterior lies free in the lumen. Heavy worm burdens cause a chronic inflammatory colitis with mucosal oedema, friability and bleeding; the resulting colorectal inflammation, chronic blood loss and, in intense infection, mechanical and inflammatory effects on the rectum contribute to dysentery, rectal prolapse, anaemia and, in children, impaired growth and development.
additionalDifferentials: Colonic polyps or other mucosal disease
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for barrel-shaped bipolar-plugged eggs
Faecal egg quantification such as Kato-Katz to gauge burden
Full blood count for anaemia and eosinophilia
Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy visualising adult worms in heavy infection
Assessment of growth and nutritional status in children
Iron studies where anaemia is present
redFlags: Trichuris dysentery syndrome with rectal prolapse in a child
Significant anaemia from chronic colonic blood loss
Growth faltering and developmental impairment with heavy burden
Severe or persistent dysenteric symptoms despite treatment
reference.prognosis: Light infections are benign; heavy infections respond to treatment with reversal of dysentery, anaemia and growth effects, although eradication may require repeated courses and reinfection is common without sanitation.
pitfalls: Expecting reliable cure from single-dose therapy, to which whipworm responds relatively poorly
Overlooking whipworm as a cause of paediatric rectal prolapse
Attributing chronic colitis to inflammatory bowel disease without stool parasitology in endemic settings
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with a benzimidazole anthelmintic (albendazole or mebendazole), favouring an extended course of mebendazole or combination with ivermectin for heavy colonic infection
Correct anaemia with iron supplementation and provide nutritional rehabilitation and growth support in affected children
In the Trichuris dysentery syndrome, reduce the worm burden with anthelmintics and manage rectal prolapse with gentle manual reduction
Confirm cure with follow-up stool microscopy and repeat treatment, as clearance in heavy infection may require repeated courses
Advise prevention through improved sanitation, hand hygiene and safe food and water, supported by community deworming programmes to limit reinfection
Involve paediatrics and infectious diseases for severe disease with dysentery, prolapse or growth and cognitive impairment
